newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares seen restrained, await oil price hike.
newsitem.headline: India shares seen restrained, await oil price hike.

text.p: An anticipated increase in government-set oil prices will keep Indian shares on a tight leash this week, but the market can take comfort from the safe passage last week of a business-friendly budget, brokers said.
Analysts expect the government to raise prices of petroleum products to partially offset a 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) deficit in the oil-pool account, which is hurting oil refiners.
India imports most of its oil but sells to domestic consumers at below world prices through a complex cross-subsidy system. The price difference is funded by the oil-pool account.

Shares of automobile, cement and steel firms are seen staying lower. But banking, pharmaceutical and software shares are seen gaining because these are unaffected by higher oil prices while refinery stocks also stand to gain.
"How soon and how steep the price hike will be would set the market trend," said Motilal Oswal, a member-broker of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE).
Other factors like rising liquidity, falling interest rates and participation of more players would help shares strengthen, he said.
"The (market) strength is evident by the participation of good quality stocks," Oswal said. "I am bullish."
"There is still a lot of room to go up, but the market will not run away," Nirmal Jain, managing director at Probity Research & Services, said.
Analysts see attention shifting to mid-cap stocks from top front-benchers because these offer greater potential gains.
"People are looking at better values in second-tier stocks," Sandeep Dhingra, equity analyst at institutional brokerage SSKI Securities told Reuters.
The BSE's benchmark index ended last week 32.37 points, or 0.85 percent, lower than the previous week at 3,769.34.
"We have an (index) target of 4,500 before the end of 1997," Dhingra said.

The Indian parliament on Friday approved the budget for 1997/98 (April-March) with its tax and tariff cuts intact, after being held hostage to political developments since its presentation on February 28.
Its approval would restore confidence in foreign investors, analysts said.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram expects the budget to spur sluggish industrial activity, but business leaders see a slow recovery in the near-term.
"The slowdown in industrial growth will bottom out only by the end of the current financial year," the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) said in a statement.
Industrial production grew by 7.5 percent in the first 10 months of 1996/97 (April-March) compared with 11.7 percent in the same period of 1995/96, government figures show.

"All the good news is history. You are now staring uncertainty in the face," said Ajit Dayal, director at Quantum Financial Services, which advises foreign funds. "...Uncertainty on the political front, monsoon and a flattish economy."
"The market's upside from here is limited -- about five percent. There should be no rush to get in," Dayal said. ($1=35.84 rupees)
